findings.description: The whole-teaching reading conflates the Third Ambassador (ⲡⲣⲉⲥⲃⲉⲩⲧⲏⲥ) with the Living Spirit and the Father of Life. In Manichaean cosmology these are distinct figures: the Living Spirit (Demiurge / Father of Life) belongs to the second evocation cycle, while the Third Messenger / Ambassador belongs to the third. Calling 'the Father of Life' an operative aspect of 'the Third Ambassador' (and treating them as one 'sending-forth' under one saying) merges two cosmic personae that the substrate keeps separate. The gap-7 restoration 'and the Living Spirit, the Father' compounds this by inserting both names into a single saying, when the surviving syntax could equally read 'of the Ambassador [of Life], whom they call Father of [Life]' — i.e. one figure (the Living Spirit/Father of Life) being called Ambassador only by epithetic appropriation, OR five distinct figures each receiving one saying.
findings.suggestion: Flag gap 7 as a doctrinally consequential restoration. Consider rewriting the second-saying paragraph in the reading so that Ambassador and Living Spirit are not flattened together; or note explicitly that the substrate distinguishes them and that the saying-2 mapping is uncertain.

findings.description: Gap 6 is restored to ⲡⲙⲁⲍϣⲁⲙⲧ ('the Third') with high confidence on the basis of normalizing the editor's reported bare ϣⲁⲙⲧ. This is a silent correction of the editor's text by appeal to a 'standard corpus form'. While ⲡⲙⲁⲍϣⲁⲙⲧ ⲙ̄ⲡⲣⲉⲥⲃⲉⲩⲧⲏⲥ is indeed the conventional title, presenting the corrected form as 'high confidence' rather than as an editorial conjecture obscures that the manuscript witness here has just ϣⲁⲙⲧ.
findings.suggestion: Downgrade gap 6 to 'moderate' or annotate that this is a normalization of the editor's reading, not a recovery of lost characters.

findings.description: Gap 1 fills 'and the [Law]' so that the opening clause becomes 'foundation for the Mind of Light and the Law'. This is self-acknowledged as low confidence and the reading itself does not exploit it (the arc treats the foundation as 'for the Mind of Light' alone, with the Law arriving only as the third saying). The restoration risks back-reading the third-saying topic into the opening frame.
findings.suggestion: Consider leaving gap 1 unrestored or note in the reading that this fill is provisional and not load-bearing.

findings.description: Gap 17 is restored ⲛⲉⲩⲣⲉⲛ ⲇⲉ 'and their names' as a 9-char subject for 'all of them, they are one body, living'. The antecedent for 'their' is awkward — the surviving text has just spoken of 'the cosmos' (singular), not of plural named figures. Marked low confidence, but the English fill is being used in the reading as the bridge into 'one living body'.
findings.suggestion: Consider leaving unrestored, or substitute a less specific subject (e.g. 'the [aeons]' or 'these [five]') and weaken the reading's reliance on it.

findings.description: The clause 'whom they themselves call: the Father of [Life]' is a reportorial / mildly polemical frame ('they call it X'). The extraction kept it because it identifies the cosmic figure being mapped. The justification is reasonable, but at corpus scale this is the kind of attributive frame ('they say', 'they call', 'they themselves') that elsewhere would be stripped. Worth noting as a borderline case where substrate-identification overrode the editorial-frame filter.
findings.suggestion: No action — flag for consistency audit across teachings where similar 'whom they call' clauses appear.

findings.description: The five-name catechesis with apophatic Father, Third Ambassador, Father of Life, First Father, the Law, the Mother sending the king of the aeons of light into Enmity, and the boundary (ⲙⲉⲑⲟⲣⲟⲛ) until the last time, is a clean Iranian-Manichaean cosmogonic scaffold visible through the Coptic. ⲡⲣⲉⲥⲃⲉⲩⲧⲏⲥ glosses Middle Persian/Parthian frēstag (the Third Messenger); ⲡϣⲁⲣⲡ ⲛⲓⲱⲧ corresponds to nxwstēn pid (Father of Greatness / First Father); the 'king of the aeons of light' is the Primal Man (ohrmizd-bay); and ⲙⲉⲑⲟⲣⲟⲛ is the eschatological boundary between the two principles. The five-saying numerology also reflects the canonical Iranian fivefold (five sons, five limbs, five elements).
findings.suggestion: Observation only; informs reading but is not a defect.

findings.description: The reading assigns each of five preserved fragments to one of five sayings (1=Father, 2=Ambassador, 3=Law, 4=Mother's gift, 5=unity in one body). The text preserves explicit ordinal markers only for the second (ⲡⲙⲁⲥⲥⲛⲉⲩ in §637) and arguably the third (ⲡⲛⲟⲙⲟⲥ launching at §641); there are no surviving 'fourth' / 'fifth' markers. The fivefold partition is therefore an interpretive reconstruction. The reading does not flag this; it presents the 1-2-3-4-5 sequence as if structurally given.
findings.suggestion: Add a sentence in the reading acknowledging that markers for sayings 4 and 5 are not preserved and that their assignment to the 'Mother' and 'one body' material is interpretive.

findings.description: Reading uses heavy Swedenborgian vocabulary ('Divine Esse', 'Grand Man', 'five degrees of reception', 'storehouses of received truth', 'inmost', 'ultimates', 'mingled state'). This is expected for a correspondential reading, but the density is unusually high here and at points imports system-specific machinery (e.g. 'five degrees' as 'standard fullness of the natural-rational interface') that is not anchored to anything in the surviving Coptic. Borderline overclaim.
findings.suggestion: Consider trimming the 'five degrees of reception' claim, which has no textual hook, and tying correspondential terms more tightly to surviving lexemes.

structural_observations.observation: The teaching is a catechetical enumeration ('five sayings') and the surviving text gives only fragmentary anchors: an ordinal 'second' at §637, the topic-noun 'the Law' at §641, a feminine-subject narrative at §643–645, and a body-image at §647–649. The pipeline has handled this well structurally, but the reading should not exceed what these anchors warrant.

13 of 19 gaps restored (≈68%), with several high-confidence fills (Mind of Light, Third Ambassador, Father of Life, members) anchored in fixed lexicon, and the genuinely indeterminate gaps (2, 3, 9, 11, 12, 14) honestly left unrestored. The mix is appropriate for a heavily damaged page.

The opening request frame 'Pronounce to us, our Lord' was correctly stripped, and the disciple-question structure typical of Kephalaia openings is no longer visible in the core. The 'whom they themselves call' clause in §639 is the only mild-frame residue retained, and the temporal note flags it.

overall_assessment: Teaching 12 is a heavily lacunose catechetical chapter on 'the five sayings' that found the Mind of Light. Extraction is solid: the disciple-question opening was properly stripped, the five-name enumeration kept as substrate, and the only retained frame ('whom they themselves call') is reasonably justified. Restoration is generally honest, with high-confidence fills tied to fixed Manichaean lexicon (Mind of Light, Father of Life, members) and proper non-restoration of genuinely indeterminate slots. The main weaknesses are in the whole-teaching reading: (1) it conflates the Third Ambassador with the Living Spirit / Father of Life under a single 'sending-forth' saying, although Manichaean cosmology distinguishes these figures; (2) it presents a 1-2-3-4-5 partition as structurally given when only the second and third ordinals are preserved; (3) it imports Swedenborgian machinery ('five degrees of reception') without textual anchor in the surviving Coptic. None of these distort the broad arc, but the reading would be more honest with explicit acknowledgement of the interpretive moves. A few low-confidence restorations (gaps 1, 17) are doing more rhetorical work in the reading than their confidence warrants."
